agency.name: New Hampshire Department of Safety, Division of Motor Vehicles

handbook.title: New Hampshire Driver's Manual
handbook.edition: DSMV 360 (Rev. 11/25), the manual PDF linked from dmv.nh.gov (PDF created 2026-01-06, modified 2026-03-03). Re-downloaded from dmv.nh.gov on Oct 15, 2026: byte-identical (SHA-256 4af2af2a...e737902) to the copy research/handbooks/NH.txt was extracted from, and to the latest Wayback capture (Sept 2, 2026). Page numbers are PDF pages (printed page number + 6). Statute, rule and DMV web-page quotes are in research/handbooks/NH_LAWS.txt (gc.nh.gov RSAs and Saf-C rules plus dmv.nh.gov pages, all retrieved Oct 15, 2026; page = that file's page marker). Motorcycle quotes are in research/handbooks/NH_MOTORCYCLE.txt (NH DMV Motorcycle Operator Manual = MSF 17th edition with NH pages, linked from the DMV motorcycle page; PDF pages).

exam.roadSigns: No separate road-signs section is described: the manual (p. 8) describes one automated test of 40 questions 'pertaining to the rules of the road and general driving conditions'; sign shapes, colors and meanings are in the manual's rules-of-the-road section.
exam.format: Automated touch-screen test (manual p. 8): 40 multiple-choice questions, each with four answers chosen by touching a letter; 40 minutes; the test ends automatically as soon as more than 8 answers are wrong (32 correct = 80% passes). The DMV testing page adds that every knowledge test has a time limit based on the number of questions, tests are specific to the license type and completely random, and an optional audio version is available with headphones.
exam.languages: English, French, Spanish, Arabic, Mandarin, Portuguese, Farsi and American Sign Language (DMV testing page); the manual says these are offered in both written and audible formats.
exam.retestWait: 10 calendar days after a failed knowledge test for Operator (car) and Motorcycle applicants (CDL: 5 calendar days).
exam.notes: Sources: manual p. 8 (40 questions, 40 minutes, test ends after more than 8 wrong); DMV Driver Licensing Testing Requirements page, Oct 15, 2026 (80% on all knowledge exams, time limit based on number of questions, languages, 10-day retest wait); rule Saf-C 1005.01-.02 (up to 50 questions, up to 60 minutes, 80% to pass, a passed knowledge test is valid one year). All tests are by appointment, and vision and knowledge tests must be passed before the road test. NH issues no learner's permit: a person 15 1/2 or older may practice with a licensed parent/guardian or licensed adult 25+ in the front seat and must carry proof of age. Licenses start at 16 as a vertical Youth Operator license (to the 21st birthday); under 18 requires approved driver education, 40 supervised hours (10 at night) and written parental consent. New residents with a valid out-of-state license take only the vision test (all three tests if the license expired more than one year ago).

motorcycleExam.notes: A motorcycle knowledge test (based on the NH DMV Motorcycle Operator Manual) plus a vision test is required for the 45-day motorcycle learner's permit ($30; one renewal). All NH knowledge exams require 80%; motorcycle applicants wait 10 calendar days to retest. The DMV skills test is waived after the Basic Rider Course; applicants under 18 must complete the Basic Rider Course and give parental permission. The number of motorcycle test questions is not published.

facts.value: 0.08% BAC or more (drivers 21 and older)
facts.detail: A driver is legally intoxicated at a blood alcohol concentration of .08% or higher. You can also be convicted below .08% if alcohol or drugs impair your ability to drive.

source.quote: It is considered legally intoxicated if a driver’s blood alcohol concentration is .08% or higher, .02% or higher if the driver is under 21 years old.

facts.value: 0.02% BAC for drivers under 21
facts.detail: Drivers under 21 break the law with an alcohol concentration of 0.02 or more, or if any alcohol, drug or other substance impairs their driving.

source.quote: It is illegal for an operator under 21 years of age to have physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or controlled drugs, prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs or any other chemical substances, natural or synthetic, which impair a person’s ability to drive or while having an alcohol concentration 0.02 or more.

facts.value: 0.04% BAC in a commercial vehicle
facts.detail: Driving a commercial vehicle with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more brings extra CDL penalties on top of the DWI penalties (RSA 265-A:23). Anyone driving a commercial motor vehicle with any alcohol in their system is placed out of service for 24 hours (RSA 265-A:24).

source.quote: or who drives a commercial vehicle with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall in addition to the penalties provided in this chapter be subject to the additional penalties and sanctions provided in RSA 263:94.

facts.value: Refusing a chemical test after a DWI arrest: 180-day license suspension for a first refusal (9 months starting Jan. 1, 2027)
facts.detail: Anyone who drives in NH has consented to blood, breath or urine testing if arrested for DWI. A first refusal brings a 180-day administrative suspension (2 years with a prior DWI or refusal); a 2026 law raises these to 9 months and 3 years starting Jan. 1, 2027. The suspension is in addition to any DWI penalty. The manual (p. 12) says only that refusal may result in loss of driving privileges.

source.quote: (a) If this is the first refusal with no prior driving or operating while intoxicated or aggravated driving or operating while intoxicated convictions: (1) The director shall suspend his or her license to drive or nonresident driving privilege for a period of 180 days; or

facts.value: Class B misdemeanor; fine of at least $500; license lost 9 months to 2 years; impaired driver education program
facts.detail: A first DWI conviction means a fine of at least $500, loss of driving privileges for 9 months to 2 years, and an approved impaired driver education program before the license is restored. Later convictions bring higher fines and longer suspensions.

source.quote: Any person who is convicted of a first offense of Driving or Operating Under Influence of Drugs or Liquor or Driving or Operating with Excess Alcohol Concentration shall be guilty of a Class B misdemeanor, fined not less than $500, may face a loss of driving privileges for a period of 9 months to 2 years, and will be required to attend an approved impaired driver education program prior to restoration of driving privileges.

facts.value: Alcohol in the passenger area only in the original sealed container; opened, capped containers go in the trunk
facts.detail: A driver may not carry alcohol in the passenger area unless it is in its original container with the seal unbroken; a securely capped, partly full container must ride in the trunk (or the area least accessible to the driver if there is no trunk). Fine $150, and a driver's license may be suspended 60 days for a first offense (RSA 265-A:44, IV). Marijuana follows the same rule (RSA 265-A:44, II-a).

source.quote: no driver shall transport, carry, possess, or have any liquor or beverage within the passenger area of any motor vehicle or OHRV upon any way in this state except in the original container and with the seal unbroken. Securely capped partially filled containers of liquor or beverages shall be stored and transported in the trunk of the motor vehicle or OHRV.

facts.value: No learner's permit; practice driving allowed from age 15 1/2
facts.detail: New Hampshire does not issue learner's permits. An unlicensed person at least 15 1/2 may practice driving with a qualified licensed adult and must carry proof of age in the vehicle.

source.quote: New Hampshire does not issue permits to learn to drive; however, New Hampshire law allows a person at least 15 ½ years of age, who does not possess a driver’s license, to drive a motor vehicle while being taught to drive

facts.value: None: New Hampshire issues no learner's permit
facts.detail: There is no permit to hold. Learners practice from age 15 1/2 with a qualified licensed adult; applicants under 18 can apply for a license at 16 after approved driver education and 40 hours of supervised driving (10 at night).

source.quote: New Hampshire does not issue permits to learn to drive

facts.value: 40 hours of supervised driving, including 10 at night
facts.detail: Applicants under 18 must log 40 hours of supervised driving (10 of them at night) in addition to driver education: 30 hours of classroom, 10 hours of driving and 6 hours of observation with a certified instructor.

source.quote: 40 hours of additional supervised driving time with a parent, guardian or other responsible adult, in which 10 hours must be completed at night.

facts.value: A licensed parent or legal guardian, or a licensed responsible adult 25 or older, in the front seat
facts.detail: A learner must be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or responsible adult 25 or older who holds a valid license and sits in the front seat (a certified driving instructor may also supervise, RSA 263:25). The supervising adult is liable for any violation the learner commits.

source.quote: when accompanied by a parent; legal guardian; or a responsible adult who is 25 years of age or older, and who is a licensed driver.

facts.value: 16 (Youth Operator license, ages 16-20)
facts.detail: Every driver 16 to under 21 receives a vertical Youth Operator license that expires on the 21st birthday. Applicants under 18 need approved driver education, 40 supervised hours and written parental consent.

source.quote: Youth Operator license holders: Any person 16 years of age or older and under the age of 21 will be issued a Youth Operator license.

facts.value: Under 18: no driving from 1:00 a.m. to 4:00 a.m.
facts.detail: A Youth Operator under 18 may not drive between 1:00 a.m. and 4:00 a.m. A first violation can bring a fine of up to $100 and a suspension of up to 30 days; later violations up to $200 and 90 days (RSA 263:14, II(d)).

source.quote: the holder of a Youth Operator License, who is under the age of 18 years of age shall NOT operate a motor vehicle: • Between the hours of 1:00 am and 4:00 am;

facts.value: First 6 months (under 18): no more than 1 passenger under 25 who is not family, unless a licensed adult 25+ rides along; never more passengers than seat belts
facts.detail: During the first six months of the license, a Youth Operator under 18 may carry only one non-family passenger under 25 unless a licensed responsible adult 25 or older is in the vehicle. Under-18 drivers may never carry more passengers than there are seat belts.

source.quote: With more than one passenger less than 25 years of age who is not a member of the driver’s family unless accompanied by a licensed, responsible adult who is at least 25 years of age during the first six (6) months holding the license;

facts.value: 18 (Youth Operator curfew, passenger and phone limits apply only under 18; the vertical Youth Operator license itself runs to the 21st birthday)
facts.detail: The 1-4 a.m. curfew, passenger limits and total phone ban end at 18. The license stays a Youth Operator license until the 21st birthday, and drivers under 20 still face extra suspensions for violations.

source.quote: In addition to any other restrictions, the holder of a Youth Operator License, who is under the age of 18 years of age shall NOT operate a motor vehicle:

facts.value: All drivers: no hand-held phones or electronic devices while driving or stopped in traffic
facts.detail: No driver may use a hand-held device while moving or while briefly stopped at a light or in traffic; holding a phone near your ear while moving is presumed to be a call. Drivers 18 and older may use hands-free devices; calling 911 is always allowed.

source.quote: no person, while driving a moving motor vehicle upon a way or temporarily halted in traffic for a traffic control device, or other momentary delay, shall use any hand-held mobile electronic device capable of providing voice or data communication

facts.value: Texting, reading or posting messages on a hand-held device is banned for all drivers
facts.detail: The hand-held ban covers reading, writing, viewing or posting messages, browsing the internet, typing into a GPS, and manually typing into any portable device. Fines are $100, $250 and $500 (within 24 months) through Dec. 31, 2026; starting Jan. 1, 2027 they are $250, $500 and $750 (more if the violation contributes to a crash), and a third offense can also bring up to a 30-day suspension.

source.quote: shall use any hand-held mobile electronic device capable of providing voice or data communication, including but not limited to: reading, composing, viewing, or posting any electronic message;

facts.value: Under 18: no phone or mobile device at all while driving, even hands-free (911 emergencies only)
facts.detail: Drivers under 18 may not use any cell phone or mobile device, hand-held or hands-free, while driving or stopped in traffic, except to report an emergency. Violations can also trigger Youth Operator license suspension.

source.quote: Drivers under the age of 18 years of age shall not use a cellular or mobile telephone or other mobile electronic device, whether hands-free or not, while driving a motor vehicle or temporarily stopped in traffic upon any way, except to report an emergency to the enhanced 911 system or any public safety agency.

facts.value: Required only for drivers and passengers under 18 (NH has no adult seat belt law)
facts.detail: New Hampshire has no seat belt requirement for adult drivers or passengers; belts are required for everyone under 18, and the driver is responsible for belting passengers under 18. Belts are still strongly recommended for all ages.

source.quote: In New Hampshire, safety restraints are required for anyone under the age of 18; however, it is highly recommended that drivers and passengers of all ages use safety restraints.

facts.value: Child safety seat until age 7 or 57 inches tall; rear-facing seat under age 2; seat belt for everyone under 18
facts.detail: A child under 7 who is shorter than 57 inches must ride in a federally approved child restraint; children under 2 must ride in a rear-facing seat (RSA 265:107-a, I-c). Fines are $50 for a first offense and $100 after that.

source.quote: A child less than 7 years old and less than 57 inches in height must be properly fastened and secured in a child passenger restraint which complies with the safety standards of the United States Department of Transportation.

facts.value: Never faster than is reasonable and prudent for conditions
facts.detail: Posted limits are the maximum for ideal conditions. You must drive slower when weather, traffic, curves, hills, intersections or pedestrians call for it.

source.quote: I. No person shall drive a vehicle on a way at a speed greater than is reasonable and prudent under the conditions and having regard to the actual and potential hazards then existing.

facts.value: 10 mph below the usual posted limit, from 45 minutes before school opens and until 45 minutes after it closes
facts.detail: In a posted school zone the limit drops 10 mph below the normal limit from 45 minutes before school opening until it opens, and from school closing until 45 minutes after closing.

source.quote: Posted School Zone – the speed limit is 10 miles per hour (mph) below the usual posted speed limit, from 45 minutes before school opening until the school opening, and from the school closing until 45 minutes after school closing.

facts.value: 30 mph in urban residence districts; 35 mph in rural residence districts
facts.detail: Unless posted otherwise, the limit is 30 mph in business and urban residence districts and 35 mph in rural residence districts (and on class V roads outside a town's compact part).

source.quote: 30 miles per hour in any business or urban residence district as defined in RSA 259:118; • 35 miles per hour in any rural residence district as defined in RSA 259:93

facts.value: 30 mph
facts.detail: The default limit in any business district is 30 mph, the same as in urban residence districts.

source.quote: 30 miles per hour in any business or urban residence district as defined in RSA 259:118;

facts.value: 55 mph (45 mph on unimproved rural highways)
facts.detail: Outside districts and interstates the default limit is 55 mph; unimproved rural highways are 45 mph. The manual summarizes this as '45 or 55 miles per hour in other locations'.

source.quote: (d) 45 miles per hour in any unimproved rural highway as defined in RSA 259:116-a. (e) 55 miles per hour in other locations, except as provided in (f);

facts.value: 65 mph on interstates and divided turnpikes; 70 mph on I-93 from mile marker 45 to the Vermont border
facts.detail: The interstate and turnpike limit is 65 mph where they are divided highways of 4 or more lanes. The only 70 mph stretch is I-93 from mile marker 45 north to the Vermont line.

source.quote: (f) 65 miles an hour on the interstate system, the central New Hampshire turnpike and the eastern New Hampshire turnpike in locations where said highways are 4-lane divided highways or other divided highways of 4 or more lanes, except that the speed limit on the portion of I-93 from mile marker 45 to the Vermont border shall be 70 miles per hour.

facts.value: 45 mph minimum on interstates (unless conditions make that unsafe)
facts.detail: On an interstate highway you may not drive slower than 45 mph unless road and weather conditions make that speed unsafe (RSA 265:64 requires the 45 mph minimum to be posted). Drivers far slower than traffic cause hazards.

source.quote: The minimum speed you may drive on an interstate highway is 45 mph, unless road and weather conditions are so bad that this speed is unsafe.

facts.value: Allowed after a full stop unless a sign prohibits it
facts.detail: Stop at the stop line, crosswalk or intersection edge, yield to pedestrians and traffic, then turn right unless a 'No Turn on Red' sign is posted.

source.quote: EXCEPTION: Drivers may make a right turn on a red signal ONLY IF there is no sign prohibiting a right turn on red.

facts.value: Not allowed (not even from a one-way onto a one-way street) unless a sign at the intersection permits the turn
facts.detail: NH's signal law lets traffic facing a steady red proceed only for a right turn on red or a turn a posted sign permits. There is no one-way-to-one-way left-on-red exception.

source.quote: (a) Vehicular traffic facing a steady circular red signal alone shall stop at a clearly marked stop line or before entering the crosswalk on the near side of the intersection or, if none, then before entering the intersection and shall remain standing until an indication to proceed is shown except as provided in subparagraphs III, (b) and (f).

facts.value: At least 100 feet before a turn; at least 500 feet before changing lanes or exiting on a highway
facts.detail: The law requires a turn signal during at least the last 100 feet before turning (RSA 265:45). On highways the manual advises signaling at least 500 feet ahead, and earlier in rain, snow or fog.

source.quote: Drivers should signal at least 100 feet before a turn, and on the highway, drivers should signal at least 500 feet before changing lanes or exiting the roadway.

facts.value: Pull to the right edge and stop until it passes (not in an intersection); never follow a fire truck closer than 500 feet
facts.detail: Yield to any emergency vehicle using a siren or flashing lights by pulling to the right and stopping clear of intersections. Do not follow a fire truck responding to an alarm closer than 500 feet, or drive or park in the block where it has stopped.

source.quote: Drivers should drive immediately to the right side of the road and stop the vehicle until the emergency has passed. Drivers should avoid blocking an intersection when stopping. Once the emergency vehicle has passed, drivers must use their signal and turn back into the roadway, only when it is safe to do so. Drivers must not follow a fire truck closer than 500 feet when it is sounding a siren or operating flashing lights.

facts.value: Sherrill's Law: slow down and, if practical, give a wide berth (or move to a lane not next to the scene) at emergencies, police stops and any stopped vehicle showing warning signals
facts.detail: Near a crash, fire, roadwork, police stop or any stopped vehicle with hazard lights, flares, cones or signs: keep a reduced speed, give a wide berth if practical without endangering oncoming traffic, obey anyone directing traffic, and leave any wholly or partly blocked lane as soon as possible. Fines: $75 for a first offense, $250 for another within 12 months (RSA 265:37-a).

source.quote: New Hampshire’s “Sherrill’s Law” law (RSA 265:37-a) requires drivers to provide a wide space or change into a lane not adjacent to certain situations if traffic conditions allow to do so safely.

facts.value: Stop at least 25 feet from a stopped school bus with red lights flashing, from either direction, unless a divided highway separates you
facts.detail: Stay stopped until the bus moves or its red lights stop flashing. On a divided highway with separate roadways, traffic on the other side need not stop (RSA 265:54, III). Passing a stopped bus on the right brings a $500 fine and a suspension of up to 30 days for a first offense (RSA 265:54, IV).

source.quote: Drivers must stop at least 25-feet in any direction for a school bus that is stopped with its red lights flashing and/or the stop arm extended at all times unless the roadway is separated by a physical barrier.

facts.value: At least 4 seconds
facts.detail: Keep at least a four-second following distance, more on slippery roads, at night, in bad weather and behind large vehicles. The manual adds at least 1 extra second at night and 2 on unfamiliar roads at night.

source.quote: Drivers should always try to keep a minimum following distance of at least four seconds between their car and the vehicle in front.

facts.value: From 1/2 hour after sunset to 1/2 hour before sunrise, and whenever rain, snow or fog keeps you from seeing 1,000 feet ahead
facts.detail: Headlights are required at night (half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise) and any time weather keeps people and vehicles from being clearly visible 1,000 feet ahead.

source.quote: New Hampshire law requires every motor vehicle driven during the period from 1/2 hour after sunset to 1/2 hour before sunrise, and whenever rain, snow, or fog shall interfere with the proper view of the road so that persons and vehicles on the way are not clearly discernible at a distance of 1000 feet ahead, shall display at least 2 lighted lamps on the front;

facts.value: Dim within about 150 feet of an approaching vehicle (RSA 265:114)
facts.detail: NH law requires dimming your headlights when approaching, overtaking or following within approximately 150 feet of another vehicle at night. The manual simply says to dim high beams for all approaching traffic.

source.quote: The driver of any vehicle upon approaching, overtaking or while following within a distance of approximately 150 feet of another vehicle on a way during the period from 1/2 hour after sunset to 1/2 hour before sunrise shall dim his headlights.

facts.value: Dim within about 150 feet when following or overtaking (RSA 265:114)
facts.detail: The same 150-foot rule applies when following or passing another vehicle at night; the manual says to use low beams whenever you follow another vehicle.

source.quote: The driver of any vehicle upon approaching, overtaking or while following within a distance of approximately 150 feet of another vehicle on a way during the period from 1/2 hour after sunset to 1/2 hour before sunrise shall dim his headlights.

facts.value: 15 feet
facts.detail: Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant.

source.quote: Within 15 feet of a fire hydrant

facts.value: 20 feet from a crosswalk at an intersection (never on a crosswalk)
facts.detail: Parking on a crosswalk or within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection is illegal even where no sign is posted.

source.quote: Within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection

facts.value: Never within an intersection (no separate distance; the 20-foot crosswalk rule applies)
facts.detail: Parking in an intersection is illegal even if unmarked. NH sets no separate distance from intersections; use the 20-foot crosswalk and 30-foot stop sign/signal rules.

source.quote: Although not marked, it is illegal to park in the following places: • Alongside another parked vehicle (no double parking) • On a sidewalk • In an intersection

facts.value: 30 feet
facts.detail: Do not park within 30 feet of a stop sign or traffic signal (the manual also lists yield signs; the statute lists flashing signals, stop signs and traffic control signals at the side of the road).

source.quote: Within 30 feet of a stop sign, yield sign or traffic control signal

facts.value: 50 feet from the nearest rail
facts.detail: Do not park within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

source.quote: Within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing

facts.value: 20 feet from a fire station driveway; 75 feet on the opposite side of the street
facts.detail: Keep 20 feet from a fire station driveway on the same side, and 75 feet from the entrance on the opposite side of the street (where signs are posted, RSA 265:69, II(e)).

source.quote: Within 20 feet of the driveway entrance to any fire station or within 75 feet on the opposite side of the street

facts.value: Within 12 inches of the curb on a one-way roadway (right wheels parallel to the right curb on two-way roads)
facts.detail: On a one-way roadway, park parallel in the direction of traffic with your wheels within 12 inches of the right or left curb. On two-way roads, park with your right wheels parallel to the right curb; the manual says to park as close to the curb as possible.

source.quote: every vehicle stopped or parked upon a one-way roadway shall be so stopped or parked parallel to the curb or edge of the roadway, in the direction of authorized traffic movement with its right-hand wheels within 12 inches of the right-hand curb or edge of the roadway, or its left-hand wheels within 12 inches of the left-hand curb or edge of the roadway.

facts.value: Stop 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail
facts.detail: When a train is coming, crossing signals flash or gates are down, stop behind the stop line or 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail. Buses carrying passengers and vehicles hauling flammable or hazardous material must stop at every crossing.

source.quote: When a train or railroad vehicle is approaching the intersection, a driver must stop behind the stop line or not less than 15 feet, nor more than 50 feet from the nearest rail of the track.

facts.value: At least 3 feet at 30 mph or less, plus 1 foot for every 10 mph above 30
facts.detail: A passing distance is presumed safe if it is at least 3 feet at 30 mph or slower, with one more foot for each 10 mph over 30 (for example, 5 feet at 50 mph).

source.quote: The distance shall be presumed to be reasonable and prudent if it is at least 3 feet when the vehicle is traveling at 30 miles per hour or less, with one additional foot of clearance required for every 10 miles per hour above 30 miles per hour.

facts.value: Yield to pedestrians in marked crosswalks and at intersections even without crosswalk lines; stop completely for a blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog
facts.detail: Pedestrians have the right of way in crosswalks and when crossing sidewalks at driveways and alleys. Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian (RSA 265:35, IV). Pedestrians without a sidewalk walk on the left, facing traffic.

source.quote: Drivers are required to yield to pedestrians crossing the road in marked crosswalks or at intersections even if no crosswalk lines exist at the intersection.

facts.value: Written report to the DMV within 15 days if anyone is killed or injured or combined property damage is over $1,000 (not needed if police investigated)
facts.detail: File the Operator Accident Report (DSMV 400) within 15 days; if a police officer investigated, the officer's report satisfies the requirement. If unsure whether damage tops $1,000, file anyway.

source.quote: New Hampshire law requires that an accident report be filed with the Division of Motor Vehicles within fifteen (15) days if there is a fatality, injuries or if the combined property damage totals more than $1,000 as a result of the accident.

facts.value: Auto insurance is not mandatory in NH; uninsured drivers must pay for crash damages or lose their license
facts.detail: You may legally drive without insurance, but after an uninsured crash you are responsible for all damages, and the DMV suspends your license until you settle; you may then need SR-22 insurance for years. If you do buy a policy, it must carry at least 25/50/25 liability, $1,000 medical payments and uninsured-motorist coverage (RSA 259:61, 264:15, 264:16).

source.quote: Almost all states require drivers to purchase automobile insurance. New Hampshire has no mandatory law, so a driver may drive a vehicle within the State of New Hampshire without insurance.

facts.value: Age 21+: 12 points in 1 calendar year = up to 3-month suspension (18 in 2 years = 6 months; 24 in 3 years = 1 year). Lower thresholds under 21
facts.detail: Convictions carry 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6 demerit points. Under 18: 6, 12 or 18 points in 1, 2 or 3 years; ages 18-20: 9, 15 or 21 points. Points are counted by violation date.

source.quote: (c) Any person 21 years of age or older who accumulates the number of demerit points specified below, in accordance with Saf-C 212.04 shall be subject to the suspension period specified: (1) For 12 demerit points in one calendar year, up to 3 months;

facts.value: Helmets required only for riders and passengers under 18
facts.detail: Operators and passengers under 18 must wear an approved helmet with a chin or neck strap; an operator who carries an unhelmeted passenger under 18 also commits a violation (RSA 265:122). Helmets are strongly recommended for everyone.

source.quote: New Hampshire law requires all riders and passengers under the age of 18 to wear helmets approved by the United States Department of Transportation.

facts.value: Prohibited
facts.detail: Riding between lanes or between rows of vehicles is illegal, and a motorcyclist may not pass in the same lane as the vehicle being passed. Two motorcycles may share one lane, but never more than two abreast.

source.quote: III. No person shall drive a motorcycle on a roadway between lanes of traffic or between adjacent lines or rows of vehicles.

notableLaws.title: Jessica's Law: clear snow and ice from your vehicle
notableLaws.summary: Since 2002, drivers must remove all snow and ice from their vehicles before driving. If snow or ice coming off a vehicle endangers people or property, the driver can be found guilty of negligent driving: $250-$500 for a first offense and $500-$1,000 after that (RSA 265:79-b).

source.quote: Since 2002, New Hampshire drivers have been legally required to clear snow and ice off their vehicles before getting on the road.

notableLaws.title: No learner's permit: the supervising adult is liable
notableLaws.summary: NH issues no learner's permit. A person 15 1/2 or older may practice in a non-commercial vehicle with a licensed parent, guardian or adult 25+ in the front seat, and must carry proof of age. The accompanying adult is liable for any motor vehicle violation the learner commits.

source.quote: The accompanying adult shall be liable for any motor vehicle violation committed by the unlicensed driver.

notableLaws.title: Drivers under 20: suspension for any moving violation conviction
notableLaws.summary: The DMV may suspend the original license of a driver under 20 after a conviction: 20-40 days for a first offense, 45-90 days for a second, and 90-180 days for a third, plus an in-person driver program before reinstatement after a third offense (ranges in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; previously fixed 20/45/90 days).

source.quote: (1) For a first offense, a minimum of 20 days, but not more than 40 days.

notableLaws.title: Youth operators: DWI, reckless driving or 30+ mph over (since Jan. 1, 2026)
notableLaws.summary: A Youth Operator convicted of DWI, reckless driving or speeding more than 30 mph over the limit cannot get a license back for at least 90 days (on top of any court suspension) and until completing an in-person driver attitude program; if the program is completed during the suspension, up to 60 days may be stayed until age 21 as long as there are no further moving violations. The manual only says such drivers 'will face additional penalties'.

source.quote: the holder of a youth operator's license who is convicted of an offense under RSA 265-A, 265:79, or convicted of a violation of RSA 265:60 in excess of 30 miles per hour above the posted speed limit, shall not be eligible for reissuance of a license for a minimum of 90 days, consecutive to any court-imposed license suspension, and until the person has completed an approved in-person driver attitude program

notableLaws.title: Aggravated DWI at 0.16 BAC or with aggravating factors
notableLaws.summary: DWI becomes aggravated DWI with a BAC of 0.16 or more, or when impaired driving is combined with speeding over 30 mph above the limit, a crash causing serious bodily injury, eluding police, a passenger under 16, a vehicle with a combined weight rating of 10,001+ lbs, or (since Jan. 1, 2026) driving on the wrong roadway of, or across the median of, a divided highway (RSA 265:26, I). It is usually a class A misdemeanor with a fine of at least $750, a mandatory jail sentence, an ignition interlock and at least 18 months' revocation; causing serious bodily injury is a class B felony with a fine of at least $1,000 (RSA 265-A:18).

source.quote: III. While having an alcohol concentration of 0.16 or more.

notableLaws.title: Drivers under 21 may not transport alcohol or marijuana
notableLaws.summary: A driver under 21 may not carry alcohol or marijuana anywhere in the vehicle, even sealed, unless accompanied by a parent, stepparent, legal guardian, grandparent, step-grandparent, legal-age spouse, domestic partner or sibling. Penalty: possible 60-day license suspension. (The manual lists only a parent, legal guardian or legal-age spouse.)

source.quote: no driver under the age of 21 shall, except when accompanied by a parent, stepparent, legal guardian, grandparent, step-grandparent, or legal age spouse, domestic partner, or sibling, transport any liquor, beverage, or marijuana in any part of a vehicle. A driver violating this section may have his or her license or privilege to drive suspended for 60 days.

notableLaws.title: Children under 2 must ride rear-facing
notableLaws.summary: Since Jan. 1, 2024, a child under 2 must be secured in a rear-facing child restraint (in addition to the car seat rule for children under 7 and under 57 inches). The manual does not mention this rule.

source.quote: I-c. No person shall drive a motor vehicle on any way while carrying as a passenger a person less than 2 years of age unless such passenger is properly fastened and secured by a rear facing child restraint system which is in accordance with safety standards.

notableLaws.title: Uninsured crash: license suspended until damages are settled
notableLaws.summary: Because insurance is optional, an uninsured driver in a crash is personally responsible for the other party's property damage and medical bills. If unable to pay, the DMV suspends the driver's privileges until a settlement is reached, and the driver may have to carry SR-22 insurance for years.

source.quote: If a driver is unable to pay for these damages and medical bills, New Hampshire law requires the Division of Motor Vehicles to suspend the driver’s driving privileges until a settlement has been reached.

notableLaws.title: If you buy auto insurance: 25/50/25 minimum liability
notableLaws.summary: A NH motor vehicle liability policy must provide at least $25,000 for injury or death of one person, $50,000 per accident, and $25,000 for property damage, plus at least $1,000 of medical payments coverage and matching uninsured-motorist coverage (RSA 264:15, 264:16). The same 25/50/25 amounts apply to SR-22 proof of financial responsibility (RSA 264:20).

source.quote: to the amount or limit of at least $25,000 on account of injury to or death of any one person, and subject to such limit as respects injury or death of one person, of at least $50,000 on account of any one accident resulting in injury to or death of more than one person, and at least $25,000 for damage to property of others

notableLaws.title: Higher phone fines from Jan. 1, 2027
notableLaws.summary: A 2026 law raises hand-held device fines from $100/$250/$500 to $250 for a first offense ($500 if it contributed to a crash), $500 for a second within 24 months ($750 with a crash), and $750 plus up to a 30-day suspension for a third ($1,000 and 60 days with a crash).

source.quote: (a) For a first offense, a fine of $250. If the violation is a contributing cause of a motor vehicle crash, the fine shall be $500.

notableLaws.title: Tougher school bus passing penalties from Jan. 1, 2027
notableLaws.summary: Through Dec. 31, 2026, failing to stop for a stopped school bus is a violation with a $150 fine for a first offense. Starting Jan. 1, 2027 it is a class B misdemeanor with a $300 fine and a mandatory 7-day suspension; a second offense is a class A misdemeanor with a fine of at least $750 and at least 30 days' revocation (unless the court finds exceptional circumstances), and bus camera footage can be used as evidence.

source.quote: a person who violates the provisions of paragraph I shall be guilty of a class B misdemeanor and shall be fined $300 plus penalty assessment for a first offense. In addition, the director shall suspend the person's license to drive or nonresident driving privilege for a period of 7 days for the first offense.

notableLaws.title: Inspections suspended; drivers must keep vehicles safe (RSA 266:8-b, May 2026)
notableLaws.summary: A 2025 law repealed annual state safety inspections effective Jan. 31, 2026. A federal court then ordered the program to continue, but with no approved vendor the DMV says the inspection program is suspended until further notice and its status may change (Feb. 13, 2026 guidance). Since May 18, 2026, driving an unsafe vehicle or one missing required equipment is a $60 violation, and police can issue a defective equipment tag giving at least 7 calendar days to make the repair (RSA 266:8-b).

source.quote: Law enforcement may issue a defective equipment tag for a vehicle it has judged unsafe or not equipped as required under this section. Such tag shall provide a minimum period of 7 calendar days in which the owner of such vehicle is required to repair the defect specified in such tag.
